home.headline:
Can your institutions coordinate
under uncertainty?
home.subtitle: Interactive simulations exploring the trade-offs of AI governance. Experience the pacing problem and coordination failures through play.
home.quickPlayDesc: You're randomly assigned a governance crisis and an institutional role with private information the others don't have. Make one decision and see how it interacts with what the other three institutions chose independently.
home.quickPlayHero: One crisis. One role. Your call.
home.pacingDesc: Individual decision-making under uncertainty. You are the director of a national AI regulatory body. Navigate four escalating crises — each forcing a real trade-off between speed and rigour.
home.govGameDesc: Four institutions. One crisis. Each has different information and different incentives. Make your call, then discover how your decision interacts with what the others chose.
home.theoryToggle: THEORY OF CHANGE — Why interactive simulations?
home.theoryP1a: Effective AI governance doesn't fail because people lack information — it fails because
home.theoryP1c: . Regulators underestimate how fast capability advances. Technologists underestimate how slowly institutions adapt. The public underestimates how much individual decisions depend on what others decide simultaneously.
home.theoryP2a: These simulations are designed to build the mental models that
home.theoryP2c: : visceral understanding of pacing trade-offs, coordination failures, and the gap between individual good decisions and collective good outcomes.
home.theoryP3a: Better mental models → more precise public demands → more robust institutional responses →
home.theoryP3b: governance that can actually keep up
home.footer: A tool for building accurate mental models of AI governance trade-offs

pacing.title: Institutional Stress Test
pacing.subtitle: The Pacing Problem Simulator
pacing.introText: You've been appointed to lead a national AI regulatory body during a period of unprecedented technological acceleration. Your institution has limited bandwidth, imperfect information, and a public that expects both safety and speed.
pacing.pacingProblemText: Technology evolves faster than institutions can adapt. Act too quickly and you risk errors, industry capture, and legitimacy crises. Act too slowly and your rules become irrelevant before they're published. There is no "correct" answer — only trade-offs.
pacing.speedDesc: Fast action risks regulatory capture and errors
pacing.credibilityDesc: Your institution's ability to shape policy
pacing.headline: 📰 HEADLINE
pacing.runTeamDesc: These simulations are designed for group workshops. Assign real roles, separate your participants, and discover how your organization thinks about AI governance trade-offs.
pacing.workshopFormats: Workshop formats available: 15-minute demo · 1-hour session · 2-hour lifecycle arc

govGame.title: The AI Governance Game
govGame.subtitle: Asymmetric Information · Collective Deliberation · Coordination Under Uncertainty
govGame.coordinationProblem: The coordination problem is the real problem.
govGame.introText: AI governance isn't about any single institution. It's about whether multiple actors with different information, different incentives, and different time horizons can act coherently under pressure.
govGame.howItWorksText: A crisis unfolds. You step into four institutional roles, each with private intelligence the others can't see. Commit each role's decision blind, then discover how your choices interact.
govGame.newsDrivenSubtitle: Scenarios grounded in recent real-world events
govGame.whatCouldBeBetter: WHAT COULD HAVE GONE BETTER? — Largest improvement opportunities
govGame.noImprovement: No single-role change would have improved the outcome. Your choices were collectively near-optimal for this scenario.
govGame.asymmetricInfo: multiple actors with asymmetric information (each actor knows things the others don't)
govGame.basedOnReporting: Based on public reporting as of
govGame.scoringNote: SCORING: Each option describes the tension it carries. Your individual choices matter, but interactions between roles generate the biggest swings, for better or worse.
govGame.roadmapDesc: Coming next: play a scenario with your team from separate devices at your own pace, with a short public statement from each role before anyone commits, and a shared reveal page you can return to for the debrief.
govGame.forFacilitatorsDesc: Assign each participant a role and physically separate them. Give 3 minutes to read intel and decide. Bring everyone together for the reveal. The "what if" analysis makes the debrief conversation concrete.

regulator.name: The Regulator
regulator.role: You set policy and have formal authority to act. Your objective is public safety and institutional credibility.
regulator.incentive: Political pressure to act fast OR appear measured. Your legitimacy depends on due process, but the crisis won't wait for process.

platform.name: The Platform
platform.role: You control content distribution and user access. Your objective is a safe, trustworthy platform ecosystem.
platform.incentive: Revenue depends on engagement and growth. Legal liability pushes toward caution. Acting alone while competitors don't costs you users.

journalist.name: The Journalist
journalist.role: You shape the public narrative through investigation and reporting. Your objective is informing the public accurately.
journalist.incentive: Editorial pressure to publish fast and first. Competitor outlets are working the same story. Speed and accuracy pull in opposite directions.

ailab.name: The AI Lab
ailab.role: You develop the technology and hold unique technical knowledge. Your objective is responsible development and deployment.
ailab.incentive: Transparency has competitive costs. Competitors who don't share safety findings gain an advantage. Legal exposure increases with disclosure.

grades.A: Exceptional coordination. Institutional actors reinforced each other and collective impact was strongly positive.
grades.A-: Strong coordination with good outcomes. Minor gaps but overall highly effective.
grades.B: Positive coordination. More synergies than conflicts, though some damage accumulated.
grades.B-: Moderate coordination. Positive intent but mixed collective outcomes.
grades.C: Isolated action. Each institution acted independently. Outcomes reflect individual choices, not coordination.
grades.C-: Weak coordination with negative drift. Independent action produced poor collective results.
grades.D: Poor coordination. Actions mostly worked against each other.
grades.D-: Very poor coordination. Significant institutional conflicts with damaging outcomes.
grades.F: Coordination failure. Actions actively undermined each other with severe consequences.

aligned.name: The Aligned Ecosystem
aligned.desc: Your institutions found ways to reinforce each other. This is the aspiration of multi-stakeholder governance, achieved in practice by very few systems. The key factor wasn't any single actor's wisdom, but the communication architecture between them.

imperfect.name: The Imperfect Coalition
imperfect.desc: More synergies than conflicts, but gaps remain. This mirrors most successful real-world governance, functional but fragile, with success depending on informal relationships rather than structural design.

fog.name: The Fog of Governance
fog.desc: Actions occurred in parallel but didn't compose. Each institution did something reasonable in isolation, but the collective effect was incoherent. This is the default state of AI governance today.

fragmentation.name: The Institutional Fragmentation
fragmentation.desc: Your institutions actively undermined each other. Actions that made sense from one perspective created cascading problems from another, precisely the failure mode that asymmetric information produces under time pressure.
